topic: Radcliffe Line 1947: the border drawn in five weeks
hook: Your border with Pakistan and Bangladesh was drawn in five weeks by a lawyer who had never visited India.
title: Why India's Border Was Drawn in 5 Weeks by a Stranger
description:
In 1947 a British lawyer named Cyril Radcliffe, who had never been to India, drew the lines that split Punjab and Bengal. This video follows the Radcliffe Line from the secret map and the flags that changed after Independence Day to the cut canals, the Wagah ceremony and the man who left. Some details, like his refused fee and burned papers, come from reported accounts and are marked that way.

#Partition #RadcliffeLine #IndiaPakistan

chapters.title: Rivers and canals cut in two

scenes.narration: Your border with Pakistan and Bangladesh was drawn in five weeks by a lawyer who had never visited India.
scenes.headline: Drawn in five weeks
scenes.sub: By a man who had never been to India

scenes.narration: He had old maps, an old census and a deadline. And he finished before the two new countries were even born.
scenes.headline: Finished before birth

scenes.narration: By the end, you'll see two famous cities split by a line, a flag swapped three days after Independence Day, and what happened to the man who drew it.
scenes.headline: What you'll see

scenes.narration: That's seven stories, and each one is stranger than the one before.
scenes.headline: Stranger each time

scenes.narration: The last one is about the mapmaker himself, and it is not what you would expect.
scenes.headline: The last one

scenes.narration: But first, the strangest choice of all: who they picked to do the job.
scenes.headline: Who got the job

scenes.narration: Chapter one. They picked him because he knew nothing about India.
scenes.headline: Chapter one

scenes.narration: Cyril Radcliffe was a British barrister. He reached India on the eighth of July, 1947, for the first time in his life.
scenes.headline: First visit, July 1947

scenes.narration: British leaders chose him partly because he had no ties to India, so nobody could call him biased.
scenes.headline: Chosen for no ties

scenes.narration: India was due to become free in about five weeks. That was his whole deadline, for a land of hundreds of millions of people.
scenes.headline: Five-week deadline

scenes.narration: He chaired two commissions, one for Punjab and one for Bengal. Each had four Indian judges, two from each side.
scenes.headline: Two commissions

scenes.narration: The judges argued for weeks and could not agree. So the final call on every disputed district fell to Radcliffe alone.
scenes.headline: Judges couldn't agree

scenes.narration: His rule looked simple on paper: Muslim-majority areas to Pakistan, the rest to India, with other factors also considered.
scenes.headline: The simple rule

scenes.narration: His main data was the census of 1941. Villages, canals, railways and farms all had to fit around those numbers.
scenes.headline: An old census

scenes.narration: He worked through the Delhi summer, mostly kept apart from the very people his lines were about to change.
scenes.headline: Kept apart

scenes.narration: A line that would decide homes for millions of people was being drawn from an office desk.
scenes.headline: Drawn from a desk

scenes.narration: And when he finished, nobody was allowed to see the result. Which brings us to chapter two.
scenes.headline: Result kept secret

scenes.narration: Chapter two. The country was free, but its borders were still a secret.
scenes.headline: Chapter two

scenes.narration: Radcliffe finished his decisions on the twelfth of August, 1947.
scenes.headline: Done on 12 August

scenes.narration: But India and Pakistan became independent on the fourteenth and fifteenth, and the map had still not been shown to anyone.
scenes.headline: Free, no map yet

scenes.narration: The award was held back and published only on the seventeenth of August, after the celebrations were over.
scenes.headline: Published 17 August

scenes.narration: One reason given is that the delay was meant to stop border arguments from spoiling Independence Day.
scenes.headline: Why the delay

scenes.narration: So for about two days, millions of people celebrated freedom without knowing which country their village was in.
scenes.headline: Which country is this?

scenes.narration: Imagine raising a flag on your roof and not knowing whether it is even your country's flag.
scenes.headline: Whose flag is it?

scenes.narration: In Punjab, families waited for news, unsure whether home would end up in India or in Pakistan.
scenes.headline: Waiting for news

scenes.narration: When the map came out, many people discovered they were on the wrong side of a line they never chose.
scenes.headline: Wrong side of the line

scenes.narration: Then came one of the largest migrations in human history. Estimates say millions crossed in both directions.
scenes.headline: Millions on the move

scenes.narration: The number of deaths is still debated. Estimates vary widely, but even the lowest are in the hundreds of thousands.
scenes.headline: The human cost

scenes.narration: That is the cost of a line drawn fast. Next, two famous cities that sit about fifty kilometres apart.
scenes.headline: Two cities next

scenes.narration: Chapter three. Two great cities, and one border between them.
scenes.headline: Chapter three

scenes.narration: Amritsar and Lahore were the two great cities of old Punjab, roughly fifty kilometres apart on the same Grand Trunk Road.
scenes.headline: 50 km apart

scenes.narration: Lahore went to Pakistan. Amritsar, home of the Golden Temple, stayed in India.
scenes.headline: Split in two

scenes.narration: Sikhs lost a great deal in this split. Nankana Sahib, the birthplace of Guru Nanak, ended up in Pakistan.
scenes.headline: Nankana Sahib

scenes.narration: Punjab itself was cut in two. Today the name means one state in India and one province in Pakistan.
scenes.headline: One Punjab, two

scenes.narration: Punjabi is spoken on both sides, with the same songs, the same food and the same jokes.
scenes.headline: Same language

scenes.narration: Many families were separated from relatives and land, and some still talk about the home they left behind.
scenes.headline: Homes left behind

scenes.narration: Today the road between the two cities runs into a border gate, and most travellers cannot simply drive through.
scenes.headline: A gate on the road

scenes.narration: If you like strange places and facts like these, subscribe, because the next chapters get stranger.
scenes.headline: Stranger ahead

scenes.narration: Here is a quick teaser: the next place had its flag swapped three days after Independence Day.
scenes.headline: A flag swapped

scenes.narration: Chapter four. Bengal, where some towns raised the wrong flag.
scenes.headline: Chapter four

scenes.narration: Radcliffe cut Bengal too. The west stayed with India, and the east became East Pakistan, which is Bangladesh today.
scenes.headline: Bengal cut in two

scenes.narration: The line did not follow rivers or hills neatly. It followed old district and village boundaries on old maps.
scenes.headline: Old maps, new line

scenes.narration: Murshidabad had a Muslim majority, yet it went to India. Khulna had a narrow Hindu majority, yet it went to East Pakistan.
scenes.headline: The big swap

scenes.narration: Historians still argue over those choices, and people on both sides of the line remember them.
scenes.headline: Still argued over

scenes.narration: On the fifteenth of August, parts of Nadia, Murshidabad and Malda reportedly flew Pakistan's flag, because the map was not yet public.
scenes.headline: Wrong flag flying

scenes.narration: After the award came out on the seventeenth, the Indian tricolour replaced it on the eighteenth.
scenes.headline: Flag changed 18 Aug

scenes.narration: Some people in those places still celebrate their Independence Day on the eighteenth of August.
scenes.headline: Independence on the 18th

scenes.narration: The Chittagong Hill Tracts, where most people were not Muslim, went to East Pakistan as well.
scenes.headline: Chittagong Hill Tracts

scenes.narration: Calcutta stayed in India with its jute mills, but most of the jute fields ended up in East Pakistan.
scenes.headline: Mills lost their fields

scenes.narration: A single line separated a city's factories from the farms that fed them.
scenes.headline: Factory versus farm

scenes.narration: And the strangest part is that rivers do not stay still for lines. The next chapter is all about water.
scenes.headline: Water next

scenes.narration: Chapter five. The line also cut through rivers and canals.
scenes.headline: Chapter five
scenes.sub: Rivers and canals cut in two

scenes.narration: Punjab means land of five rivers, and the irrigation network built there by the British was among the largest in the world.
scenes.headline: Land of five rivers

scenes.narration: Suddenly a border drawn on paper ran across canals that had been built to serve one single province.
scenes.headline: A line over canals

scenes.narration: The headworks that sent water out could end up on one side, while the fields that needed it lay on the other.
scenes.headline: Water and fields apart

scenes.narration: Within months a dispute broke out over who controlled that water, and it dragged on for years.
scenes.headline: The water dispute

scenes.narration: In 1960, India and Pakistan signed the Indus Waters Treaty to share the rivers.
scenes.headline: Indus Waters Treaty

scenes.narration: The World Bank helped broker it. That shows how seriously a line across a canal can be taken.
scenes.headline: World Bank steps in

scenes.narration: A border drawn in five weeks took thirteen years to settle, just on the question of water.
scenes.headline: 5 weeks, 13 years

scenes.narration: Even today, some farmers in Punjab have fields beyond the border fence, and they must go through a gate to reach them.
scenes.headline: Fields beyond the fence

scenes.narration: That is the farming side of the story. Now for the one place where the line becomes a show.
scenes.headline: Where it's a show

scenes.narration: Chapter six. The one place where the Radcliffe Line becomes a daily performance.
scenes.headline: Chapter six

scenes.narration: At Attari-Wagah, on the Grand Trunk Road between Amritsar and Lahore, crowds gather every single evening.
scenes.headline: A crowd every evening

scenes.narration: Indian and Pakistani soldiers march in sharp, high-kicking steps towards the gate while the crowds cheer on both sides.
scenes.headline: High-kicking march

scenes.narration: Then the two flags are lowered at the same moment, and the gates are shut for the night.
scenes.headline: Flags down together

scenes.narration: The same line that took five weeks to draw now draws crowds every single day.
scenes.headline: The line as a show

scenes.narration: A border drawn by a stranger has become something people travel for hours to watch.
scenes.headline: People travel to see it

scenes.narration: Strange as that is, the strangest part of this story is still ahead. It is about the man himself.
scenes.headline: About the man

scenes.narration: Chapter seven. The mapmaker who left.
scenes.headline: Chapter seven

scenes.narration: Radcliffe left India around Independence Day, and accounts say he never came back.
scenes.headline: He left, never returned

scenes.narration: He reportedly refused his fee of forty thousand rupees, and did not want to be paid for the line.
scenes.headline: Refused his fee

scenes.narration: He also reportedly burned his papers before leaving, so the thinking behind many of his choices was never fully explained.
scenes.headline: Papers burned

scenes.narration: Not every detail is documented, but accounts agree he was troubled by the violence that followed his map.
scenes.headline: Troubled by what followed

scenes.narration: Think about it: one man spent five weeks on a map, and millions of people still live with it every day.
scenes.headline: Five weeks, millions of lives

scenes.narration: That is the line behind your border with Pakistan and Bangladesh: a stranger, a deadline and an old census.
scenes.headline: A stranger and a deadline

scenes.narration: Next in this series, more places where one line on a map cuts through real life. And it all began with a lawyer who had never visited India.
scenes.headline: Next: more strange lines
